Anterior cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae anteriores ossis ethmoidei lie behind the Os lacrimale and medial to the lamina orbitalis, with the Pars orbitalis ossis frontalis as the roof, and drain to the middle meatus. Pitfall: a low or asymmetric lateral lamella of the cribriform plate (Keros III) is easy to miss on axial images; check coronal reconstructions.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Arytenoid cartilage.note: Cartilago arytenoidea sits on the upper border of the Lamina cartilaginis cricoideae. Its Processus vocalis marks the level of the true vocal cord. Pitfall: asymmetric ossification or sclerosis is normal and must not be read as tumour invasion. Head rotation can also simulate arytenoid dislocation; compare cricoarytenoid joint congruence.
landmarks: lm:Articular surface of arytenoid cartilage|Arytenoid cartilage

Calcaneus.note: Articulates with the talus at the posterior, middle and anterior subtalar facets, which are separated by the sinus tarsi. It meets the cuboid anteriorly, and the tendo calcaneus inserts on the tuber calcanei. The flexor hallucis longus runs under the sustentaculum tali. Pitfall: the normal trabecular-poor neutral triangle mimics a cyst or lipoma. Also, anterior process fractures are easily missed.
passing: Calcaneal branches of posterior tibial artery
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of calcaneus|Calcaneus

Capitate bone.note: The largest carpal bone. Its head sits in the lunate concavity, it lies between the trapezoid and hamate, and it bears the third metacarpal base. Pitfall: an os styloideum (carpal boss) at the dorsal second/third CMC joint mimics a fracture. Also exclude a scaphocapitate fracture-dislocation, where the capitate head is rotated.

Clavicle.note: The sternal end articulates with the clavicular notch of the manubrium and the acromial end with the acromion. The coracoclavicular ligaments attach to the inferior surface, and the subclavian vessels and brachial plexus lie beneath. Pitfall: the medial epiphysis stays unfused until about age 25 and can look like a fracture or a physeal separation.
passing: Anterior division of middle trunk of brachial plexus

Corniculate cartilage.note: Cartilago corniculata sits on the Apex cartilaginis arytenoideae within the posterior aryepiglottic fold, next to the piriform recess of the laryngopharynx. Pitfall: when calcified, this small dense focus is easily mistaken for an ingested foreign body or a calcified node. Its paired, symmetric position on the arytenoid apex identifies it.
neighbours: Ary-epiglottic part of oblique arytenoid muscle

Cricoid cartilage.note: Cartilago cricoidea is the only complete ring of the airway, at C6 level. It has an anterior Arcus and a tall posterior Lamina that carries the arytenoids, with the trachea below and the oesophageal inlet behind. Pitfall: patchy, asymmetric ossification mimics fracture or tumour invasion. Compare with the contralateral side and the adjacent soft tissue.

Cuboid bone.note: Lateral column bone between the calcaneus and the bases of the fourth/fifth metatarsals. It articulates medially with the lateral cuneiform and sometimes the navicular. The fibularis longus tendon grooves its plantar surface. Pitfall: an os peroneum next to the tuberositas ossis cuboidei mimics an avulsion fragment. Also look for a subtle compressive 'nutcracker' fracture.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint, where flexor digitorum longus inserts on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: fusion of the middle and distal phalanges of the fifth toe (biphalangeal toe) is a common variant, not ankylosis or a missing bone.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint. The flexor digitorum profundus inserts on the palmar base and the terminal extensor tendon on the dorsal base, and the tuft lies under the nail bed. Pitfall: Kirner deformity (palmar-radial curving of the fifth distal phalanx) and normal tuft irregularity mimic a fracture. Look for cortical breaks and soft-tissue swelling.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of first finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of first finger of foot
Distal phalanx of first finger of foot.note: The great toe has only two phalanges. The distal phalanx articulates with the proximal phalanx at the single interphalangeal joint, and flexor hallucis longus inserts on its plantar base. Pitfall: an interphalangeal sesamoid on the plantar side of the joint mimics an avulsion fragment. Its smooth corticated outline tells them apart.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Articular capsule of interphalangeal joint of great toe

Distal phalanx of first finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of first finger of hand
Distal phalanx of first finger of hand.note: The thumb has only two phalanges, so this phalanx articulates directly with the proximal phalanx at the IP joint. The flexor pollicis longus inserts palmar and the extensor pollicis longus dorsal. Pitfall: a sesamoid at the palmar IP joint can be taken for an avulsion fragment. Also avoid calling this joint a 'DIP' in reports.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint and receives flexor digitorum longus on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: a fused middle and distal phalanx is a normal variant. A tuft fracture from crush injury is easily missed without thin reformats.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint, with the flexor digitorum profundus inserting at the palmar base and the terminal extensor dorsal. Pitfall: the ring finger is the classic site of FDP avulsion (jersey finger). A small palmar basal fragment may have retracted proximally along the flexor sheath, so look beyond the joint.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of second finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of second finger of foot
Distal phalanx of second finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint and receives flexor digitorum longus on the plantar side and the extensor digitorum longus tendon dorsally. Pitfall: in a flexed or clawed toe, oblique slices make the DIP joint look subluxed. Judge alignment on reformats along the axis of the ray.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of deep fibular nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of second finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of second finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of second finger of hand
Distal phalanx of second finger of hand.note: Lies distal to the DIP joint. The terminal extensor tendon inserts on the dorsal base and the flexor digitorum profundus on the palmar base. Pitfall: a dorsal basal avulsion (bony mallet) can be tiny and is easily missed on axial slices. Check sagittal reformats for the fragment and for palmar subluxation of the phalanx.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Middle phalanx of second finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Distal phalanx of third finger of foot.key: Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
Distal phalanx of third finger of foot.note: The distal phalanx runs from its base at the DIP joint, with flexor digitorum longus inserting on the plantar side, to the tuberositas phalangis distalis at the tip. Pitfall: the irregular tuft normally looks frayed or pointed and should not be read as erosion or acro-osteolysis.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
landmarks: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of foot|Distal phalanx of third finger of foot
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Distal phalanx of third finger of hand.key: Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
Distal phalanx of third finger of hand.note: Base articulates with the middle phalanx at the DIP joint; flexor digitorum profundus inserts palmar, the terminal extensor tendon dorsal at the base, distally the tuberositas phalangis distalis. Pitfall: a small dorsal-base avulsion (bony mallet) is easily missed on axial slices; use sagittal reformats and do not confuse normal tuft irregularity with a fracture.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
landmarks: lm:Tuberosity of distal phalanx of hand|Distal phalanx of third finger of hand
neighbours: Middle phalanx of third finger of hand
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints

Eighth rib.note: False rib. Its head articulates with T7 and T8 at the T7–T8 disc, and its costal cartilage joins the cartilage of the seventh rib, not the sternum. Pitfall: fractures of ribs 8–11 call for a search for liver or spleen injury and pneumothorax. Count ribs from the first rib, not from the costal margin.

Eleventh rib.note: Floating rib with a single facet for T11, no costotransverse articulation and a free tapered tip within the abdominal wall muscles. Pitfall: the free tip can be mistaken for a fracture fragment or a calcified abdominal wall lesion. Fractures here call for a check of the kidney, spleen and liver.

Ethmoid bone.note: The cribriform plate sits in the Incisura ethmoidea of the frontal bone. The lamina orbitalis (papyracea) forms the medial orbital wall, and the posterior cells border the sphenoid sinus. Pitfall: the lateral lamella of the cribriform plate is the thinnest part of the skull base. Report Keros depth, and do not read a thin or dehiscent lamina papyracea as a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Femur.note: Os femoris runs from caput ossis femoris in the acetabulum through the collum and trochanters to the corpus and the condyles, which articulate with tibia and patella. Pitfall: the fovea capitis is a normal central notch, not erosion or osteonecrosis. A small herniation pit in the anterosuperior neck is also benign.
landmarks: lm:Fovea for ligament of head of femur|Femur

Fibula.note: Caput fibulae articulates with the tibia at the superior tibiofibular joint, and the common fibular nerve winds around the neck. Distally, malleolus lateralis sits in the incisura fibularis and against the talus. Pitfall: a syndesmotic ankle injury may come with a proximal fibular (Maisonneuve) fracture, so check the whole bone. An os subfibulare mimics avulsion.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of fibula|Fibula

Fifth metacarpal bone.note: Base articulates with Os hamatum and the fourth metacarpal base, where extensor carpi ulnaris inserts; the head forms the fifth MCP joint. Pitfall: in a boxer's neck fracture, check for an associated 4th/5th carpometacarpal dorsal dislocation, which is easily overlooked on axial images; confirm hamate–metacarpal congruity on sagittal reformats.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Fifth metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuboideum and MT IV, and fibularis brevis inserts on the tuberositas. The caput articulates with the proximal phalanx. Pitfall: the longitudinal tuberosity apophysis in adolescents, or an os vesalianum, mimics avulsion. Also tell a zone-1 avulsion from a Jones fracture at the metadiaphyseal junction.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot

Fifth rib.note: True rib that articulates with T4 and T5 and connects to the sternum through its costal cartilage. Laterally it lies deep to serratus anterior, and posteriorly it lies under the scapula. Pitfall: irregular calcification at the costochondral junction mimics a fracture or a destructive lesion. Compare it with the opposite side.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

First metacarpal bone.note: Base forms the saddle joint with Os trapezium; abductor pollicis longus inserts radially, the head forms the thumb MCP joint. Pitfall: distinguish Bennett (two-part intra-articular, volar-ulnar fragment stays, shaft subluxes radially/dorsally) from Rolando (comminuted) and extra-articular base fractures; always state CMC subluxation.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of hand

First metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuneiforme mediale and receives the tibialis anterior and fibularis longus. The caput articulates with the proximal phalanx and the sesamoids. Pitfall: there is no interosseous ligament between MT I and MT II. Widening between their bases, or between the medial cuneiform and MT II, indicates a Lisfranc injury.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Proper plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot
Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis

First rib.note: Short, broad, flat rib that articulates only with T1. The tuberculum musculi scaleni anterioris separates the groove for the vena subclavia (anterior) from the groove for the arteria subclavia and plexus (posterior), and the pleural cupula lies beneath. Pitfall: a cervical rib or long C7 transverse process can be miscounted as the first rib. Confirm by its T1 articulation.

Fourth metacarpal bone.note: Base articulates mainly with Os hamatum, variably with Os capitatum, and with the third and fifth metacarpal bases; the head forms the fourth MCP joint. Pitfall: the thin shaft's oblique nutrient canal mimics a nondisplaced fracture; a true fracture breaches both cortices or shows a step.
passing: Common palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of hand

Fourth metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the os cuboideum, the lateral cuneiform, MT III and MT V. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx IV. Pitfall: diaphyseal stress fractures may show only subtle periosteal reaction. Also check that the medial cortex of the MT IV base lines up with the medial edge of the cuboid; malalignment points to a tarsometatarsal injury.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Common plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot

Fourth rib.note: True rib that articulates with T3 and T4. Anteriorly it lies under pectoralis major and minor, laterally under serratus anterior, and posteriorly under the scapula. Pitfall: posterior fractures are hidden by the overlying scapula and run nearly parallel to the axial plane. Review curved reformats or 3D reconstructions.

Frontal bone.note: The squama meets the parietal bones at the coronal suture. The orbital parts form the orbital roofs around the Incisura ethmoidea, and the frontal sinus lies between the anterior and posterior tables. Pitfall: hyperostosis frontalis interna (symmetric, spares the midline) is a normal variant. Do not mistake it for meningioma or Paget disease.
landmarks: lm:Foramen caecum of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Hamate bone.note: Distal-row carpal between Os capitatum (radial) and Os triquetrum (proximal-ulnar), bearing the 4th/5th metacarpals; the hamulus forms the ulnar wall of the carpal tunnel and the radial wall of Guyon's canal. Pitfall: hook fracture versus os hamuli proprium—an accessory ossicle has smooth corticated margins; assess on axial carpal-tunnel slices.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Opponens digiti minimi muscle of hand

Hip bone.note: Formed by the ilium, ischium and pubis, which meet at the acetabulum. It meets the sacrum at the facies auricularis and the opposite side at the symphysis. The superior gluteal vessels exit through the greater sciatic notch. Pitfall: an unfused triradiate cartilage, an os acetabuli or apophyses (AIIS, ischial) in young patients mimic fractures or avulsions.

Humerus.note: Caput humeri articulates with the glenoid; the distal condylus humeri articulates with radius and ulna, flanked by the epicondyles. Pitfall: mid-to-distal shaft fractures involving the sulcus nervi radialis threaten the radial nerve, and the surgical-neck/greater-tubercle region the axillary nerve—name the fracture's relation to these grooves.
neighbours: Scapular spinal part of deltoid muscle

Hyoid bone.note: Os hyoideum lies at C3 level. Suprahyoid muscles insert above it and the Membrana thyrohyoidea connects it to the thyroid cartilage below. The Cornu majus points backward toward the pharyngeal wall. Pitfall: an unfused synchondrosis between the body and Cornu majus, often asymmetric, mimics a fracture. Look for corticated margins and the absence of soft-tissue swelling.
landmarks: lm:Greater horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone
lm:Lesser horn of hyoid bone|Hyoid bone

Incus.note: Corpus incudis lies in the epitympanic recess behind caput mallei, forming the axial 'ice-cream cone'. Crus longum descends parallel to manubrium mallei to the processus lenticularis, which articulates with stapes. Pitfall: the thin crus longum and processus lenticularis often show partial-volume loss, which mimics erosion or incudostapedial discontinuity.

Inferior nasal concha bone.note: This separate bone attaches to the medial wall of the maxilla and the perpendicular plate of the palatine bone. It roofs the inferior meatus, where the Ductus nasolacrimalis opens. Pitfall: the nasal cycle swells one side's turbinate mucosa, and this asymmetry should not be reported as a mass or polyp.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.

Intermediate cuneiform bone.note: The smallest cuneiform. It lies between the medial and lateral cuneiforms, the navicular proximally and the second metatarsal base distally. Because it is short, the second metatarsal base is recessed into a mortise. Pitfall: subtle Lisfranc injury. Look for widening between the medial and intermediate cuneiforms, or medial cuneiform–second metatarsal diastasis, and small avulsion flecks.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot

Lacrimal bone.note: This bone forms the posterior half of the lacrimal fossa (posterior lacrimal crest), with the frontal process of the maxilla in front and the lamina orbitalis of the ethmoid behind. The lacrimal sac sits in the fossa. Pitfall: the bone is paper-thin, so partial volume can make it look dehiscent or fractured. Check the agger nasi cell, which lies medial to it.
landmarks: lm:Orbital part of frontal bone|Frontal bone

Lateral cuneiform bone.note: Lies between the intermediate cuneiform and the cuboid, with the navicular proximally. Distally it meets mainly the third metatarsal base and touches the second and fourth. Pitfall: the many overlapping tarsometatarsal joint lines on oblique slices can hide or mimic fracture lines. Check intermediate column alignment in Lisfranc injuries on reformats.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
landmarks: lm:Base of metatarsal bone|Third metatarsal bone

Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.key: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage
Lateral process of nasal septal cartilag.note: Processus lateralis cartilaginis septi nasi (the upper lateral cartilage) lies under the caudal edge of the Os nasale and merges with the septal cartilage. It forms the internal nasal valve. Pitfall: the bone–cartilage junction (keystone area) has an irregular, non-ossified edge that must not be reported as a nasal bone fracture. It is not visible in bone window.

lm:Mastoid process|Temporal bone.note: The Processus mastoideus is the pneumatized downward projection of the Os temporale, behind the external acoustic meatus. The Musculus sternocleidomastoideus, splenius capitis and longissimus capitis attach to it, and the posterior belly of the digastric arises from the Incisura mastoidea on its medial side. Pitfall: mastoid pneumatization varies widely and is often asymmetric. A sclerotic or poorly pneumatized mastoid should not be read as mastoiditis, and normal suture lines or vascular channels (mastoid emissary vein) should not be called fractures. Always confirm laterality.
landmarks: lm:Tympanic part of temporal bone|Temporal bone

Lower canine.note: The lower canine (FDI 33/43) has the longest root in the anterior mandible, lying between the lateral incisor and the first premolar, with the incisive branch of the Nervus alveolaris inferior below its apex. Pitfall: the nearby Foramen mentale can simulate a periapical lucency. Confirm continuity with the mandibular canal before diagnosing periapical disease.
passing: Mental branch of inferior alveolar artery

Lower first molar tooth.note: Two-rooted molar (mesial and distal roots) seated in the alveolar part of the mandibula, with the canalis mandibulae running below the apices. Thin lingual cortex: abscess spreads to the sublingual or submandibular space depending on mylohyoid level. Pitfall: do not mistake the canalis mandibulae or a normal interradicular trabecular gap for a periapical lucency.
landmarks: lm:Root of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Crown of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Occlusal surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth
lm:Lingual surface of tooth|Lower first molar tooth

Lower first premolar.note: Single-rooted tooth between the canine and the second premolar in the alveolar part of the mandibula. Its buccal cortex lies deep to the depressor anguli oris. Pitfall: the anterior loop of the canalis mandibulae and the canalis incisivus near the apex look like periapical lucencies. Follow them on curved reformats before calling a lesion.

Lower lateral incisor.note: The lower lateral incisor (FDI 32/42) sits in thin alveolar bone between the medial incisor and the canine, with the Fovea sublingualis on the lingual side. Pitfall: the labial and lingual cortical plates are very thin, so partial volume can mimic fenestration or a root fracture. Confirm laterality with FDI numbering on axial versus 3D views.

Lower medial incisor.note: The lower medial incisor (FDI 31/41) flanks the midline symphysis, with the genial spines and the Musculus genioglossus/geniohyoideus attachments behind it. Pitfall: midline lingual foramina and vascular canals can mimic a symphyseal fracture or periapical lesion. These canals are corticated and lie in the midline.

Lower second molar tooth.note: Two-rooted molar distal to the first molar. Its apices sit close to the canalis mandibulae and the thin lingual cortex, below the linea mylohyoidea, so infection spreads into the submandibular space. Pitfall: when teeth are missing or a third molar is unerupted, the tooth number is easy to get wrong. Count from the midline and use FDI notation (37/47).

Lower second premolar.note: Single-rooted tooth between the first premolar and the first molar. The foramen mentale usually lies just below or between the premolar apices. Pitfall: on axial CT the foramen mentale can mimic a periapical lesion or an osteolytic defect. Trace its continuity with the canalis mandibulae.

Lunate bone.note: Central proximal-row carpal in the radial lunate fossa, between Os scaphoideum and Os triquetrum, capped by Os capitatum distally and facing the TFCC ulnarly. Pitfall: lunate/perilunate dislocation is missed on axial slices—check radius–lunate–capitate collinearity and lunate tilt (DISI/VISI) on sagittal reformats.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Major alar cartilage.note: Cartilago alaris major forms the nasal tip and ala around the nasal vestibule. Its medial crus lies alongside the caudal septum and its lateral crus lies below the upper lateral cartilage. Pitfall: it has soft-tissue density and is invisible in bone window, so nasal tip injury must be assessed in soft-tissue window.
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Malleus.note: Caput mallei sits in the epitympanum in front of corpus incudis. Manubrium mallei is embedded in the membrana tympanica, and processus lateralis bounds Prussak space below the scutum. Pitfall: the tensor tympani tendon or chorda tympani can be mistaken for the manubrium, and the normal malleoincudal joint line is not a fracture.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of malleus|Malleus

Mandible.note: The Corpus mandibulae carries the Canalis mandibulae containing the Nervus alveolaris inferior, which exits at the Foramen mentale below the premolars. The Linea mylohyoidea separates the sublingual space from the submandibular space. Pitfall: the mandibular canal, mental foramen or lingual foramina can mimic fracture lines. Trace them in 3D. Mandible fractures are often paired (e.g. symphysis plus contralateral condyle).

Maxilla.note: The body encloses the maxillary sinus, with the infraorbital canal in its roof and the alveolar process below. The palatine process forms the anterior hard palate. Pitfall: vascular grooves for the posterior superior alveolar artery in the posterolateral wall can look like fracture lines, and so can molar roots projecting into the sinus floor.

Medial cuneiform bone.note: The largest cuneiform. It lies between the navicular and the first metatarsal base, and the tibialis anterior and fibularis longus insert on it. Its lateral surface anchors the Lisfranc ligament to the second metatarsal base. Pitfall: a bipartite medial cuneiform (dorsal/plantar halves separated by a smooth cleft) mimics a fracture.

Middle cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae mediae lie between the anterior and posterior groups. Laterally a thin lamina orbitalis separates them from the Musculus rectus medialis, and the Os frontale forms the roof. Pitfall: a congenitally dehiscent lamina orbitalis with herniated orbital fat can mimic a blowout fracture. Look for acute signs such as haemorrhage or emphysema.

Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Middle phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: The middle phalanx lies between the PIP and DIP joints, and flexor digitorum brevis inserts on its plantar side. On the fifth toe it is tiny and often rudimentary. Pitfall: fusion with the distal phalanx (symphalangism) is a frequent normal variant and should not be read as post-traumatic ankylosis or a missing bone.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Middle phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Between the PIP and DIP joints; flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the palmar shaft, the central extensor slip on the dorsal base. Pitfall: a short, trapezoid middle phalanx (brachymesophalangy, clinodactyly) or DIP symphalangism is a common normal variant of the fifth digit—do not report it as fracture or ankylosis.
passing: Proper palmar digital branches of ulnar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of ulnar nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Distal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints
Humero-ulnar head of flexor digitorum superficialis

Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot.key: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Middle phalanx of fourth finger of foot.note: The middle phalanx lies between the PIP and DIP joints, with flexor digitorum brevis inserting on the plantar side and the extensor tendon running dorsally. Pitfall: this short bone can fuse with the distal phalanx as a normal variant. In a flexed toe, partial volume can hide a fracture, so check reformats along the toe.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Distal phalanx of fourth finger of foot
Articular capsules of proximal interphalangeal joints of foot
Articular capsules of distal interphalangeal joints of foot

Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand.key: Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand
Middle phalanx of fourth finger of hand.note: Between the PIP and DIP joints; the palmar plate attaches to the palmar base, and flexor digitorum superficialis inserts on the shaft. Pitfall: a tiny volar plate avulsion at the palmar base is easily lost in partial volume; check sagittal reformats and report dorsal PIP subluxation.

The flexor digitorum brevis inserts plantarly on it, with the flexor digitorum longus tendon passing beneath. Pitfall: toes lie flexed, so axial slices cut the phalanges obliquely. A partial-volume overlap at the IP joints can mimic a fracture line or fusion, so check sagittal reformats.

Pitfall: a dorsal-base avulsion (central slip, boutonnière precursor) is often overlooked next to palmar plate fragments; inspect both dorsal and palmar base margins on sagittal reformats.

The flexor digitorum longus/brevis lie plantar and the extensor digitorum longus tendon lies dorsal. Pitfall: counting the toes wrongly on axial images. Count from the hallux on a coronal or 3D view before you assign a digit.

Pitfall: a pilon-type intra-articular base fracture can look minor axially—quantify articular surface involvement and dorsal subluxation on sagittal reformats.

Nasal bone.note: The paired nasal bones articulate with the frontal bone above, the frontal processes of the maxillae laterally and each other in the midline. The upper lateral cartilages attach to their inferior edges. Pitfall: the nasomaxillary suture and the groove for the external nasal nerve can look like fractures. Displacement or soft-tissue swelling supports a true fracture.
landmarks: lm:Nasal spine of frontal bone|Frontal bone
lm:Nasal part of frontal bone|Frontal bone
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Nasal septal cartilage.note: Cartilago septi nasi forms the anterior septum. Posteroinferiorly it joins the Vomer and the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid, and it rests on the maxillary crest. Pitfall: a cartilaginous septal fracture or haematoma is missed in bone window. Check soft-tissue window for bilateral septal thickening, and do not confuse a normal chondro-vomerine spur with a fracture.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
neighbours: Lateral process of nasal septal cartilage

Navicular bone.note: Articulates proximally with the caput tali and distally with the three cuneiforms. The tibialis posterior inserts on the tuberositas ossis navicularis, and the spring ligament supports it plantarly. Pitfall: an accessory navicular (os tibiale externum) mimics a tuberosity avulsion. Also, central-third stress fractures are sagittal and subtle on axial slices.

Ninth rib.note: False rib that articulates with T8 and T9. Its cartilage joins the costal margin, and the diaphragm and pleural recess lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: nutrient canals and the costal groove can mimic a non-displaced fracture on axial slices. Confirm a fracture on curved or MIP reformats before reporting it.

Occipital bone.note: The bone surrounds the foramen magnum. The basilar part forms the clivus up to the spheno-occipital synchondrosis, and the squama meets the parietal bones at the lambdoid suture. Pitfall: do not confuse the condylar canal (an emissary channel behind the condyle) with the hypoglossal canal, which runs above the condyle and carries CN XII.
landmarks: lm:Basilar part of occipital bone|Occipital bone

Palatine bone.note: The horizontal plate forms the posterior hard palate behind the maxilla. The perpendicular plate forms the medial wall of the pterygopalatine fossa and the sphenopalatine foramen. Pitfall: the greater palatine canal and foramen are a perineural spread route. Do not mistake them for the lesser palatine foramina or for erosion.
passing: Posterior lateral nasal branches of sphenopalatine artery.

Parietal bone.note: It is bounded by the sagittal, coronal, lambdoid and squamosal sutures, and its mastoid angle touches the sigmoid sinus groove. Pitfall: parietal foramina, accessory parietal sutures (in children) and arachnoid granulations can look like fractures or lytic lesions. Check the 3D reconstructions and compare with the other side.

Patella.note: The patella is a sesamoid in the quadriceps tendon and articulates with the facies patellaris femoris. The retinacula attach to its medial and lateral margins, and the infrapatellar fat pad lies below the apex. Pitfall: bipartite patella (superolateral fragment, smooth corticated margins, often bilateral) mimics a fracture.

Pisiform bone.note: Sesamoid within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon; it articulates only dorsally with Os triquetrum and forms the ulnar wall of Guyon's canal. Pitfall: fragmented or multiple ossification centres in adolescents mimic fracture; also assess the pisotriquetral joint, a frequently overlooked source of ulnar wrist pain and arthrosis.
neighbours: Humeral head of flexor carpi ulnaris

Posterior cells of ethmoid bone.note: Cellulae posteriores lie behind the basal lamella and in front of the Os sphenoideum, and drain to the superior meatus. The Arteria ethmoidea posterior runs along their roof. Pitfall: an Onodi (sphenoethmoidal) cell extends above the sphenoid sinus around the optic canal and can be mistaken for the sphenoid sinus. This poses a surgical risk to the optic nerve.
passing: Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery

Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.key: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of foot.note: Runs from the fifth MTP joint to the PIP joint. Abductor digiti minimi and flexor digiti minimi insert at its base. Pitfall: middle–distal symphalangism is common in the fifth toe and makes it look two-phalanged. Do not report a fused or 'missing' phalanx as a fracture or amputation.
passing: Proper plantar digital branches of lateral plantar nerve

Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.key: Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand
Proximal phalanx of fifth finger of hand.note: Between the fifth MCP and PIP joints; abductor and flexor digiti minimi insert on the ulnar base. Pitfall: in children the basal physis lies at the base—do not mistake it for a fracture, yet look for Salter–Harris II ('extra-octave') fractures with ulnar angulation.

Proximal phalanx of first finger of foot.note: Lies between the first MTP joint (sesamoids plantar to the metatarsal head) and the hallux IP joint. The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs plantar and the extensor hallucis longus dorsal. Pitfall: an interphalangeal sesamoid plantar to the IP joint, or a bipartite basal apophysis in adolescents, can mimic an avulsion fragment.

Pitfall: an ulnar-base avulsion (ulnar collateral ligament, skier's thumb) must not be dismissed as a palmar MCP sesamoid.

Pitfall: the toes of the third to fifth rays overlap and lie flexed on axial slices. Confirm the digit by tracing it back to its metatarsal before reporting a fracture.

Pitfall: spiral or oblique shaft fractures can hide rotational malalignment (scissoring) that looks minor axially—compare the rotation of the condyles with the adjacent digits.

Pitfall: in hammer or claw toe, the base subluxes dorsally on the second metatarsal head. On oblique axial slices this mimics a joint or fracture abnormality, so assess MTP alignment on sagittal views.

Pitfall: a collateral-ligament avulsion at the basal corner can be confused with the normal radial palmar sesamoid of the index MCP joint—sesamoids are round, corticated and lie palmar to the metacarpal head.

Pitfall: a nutrient canal in the corpus phalangis can be mistaken for a nondisplaced fracture. A true fracture usually crosses the cortex transversely or obliquely and shows soft-tissue swelling.

Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand.note: The base forms the third MCP joint and the distal trochlea phalangis forms the PIP joint. Pitfall: unicondylar fractures of the trochlea run sagittally and are nearly invisible on axial images—check coronal reformats for condylar step-off and angular deformity.

Radius.note: Caput radii articulates with the capitulum and the ulnar radial notch; distally the carpal surface bears scaphoid and lunate, and the incisura ulnaris forms the DRUJ. Pitfall: in a shaft or head fracture, assess both radioulnar joints (Galeazzi, Essex-Lopresti); the deep radial nerve winds around the neck.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint

Scaphoid bone.note: Bridges both carpal rows: proximal pole in the radial scaphoid fossa, distal pole facing Os trapezium/trapezoideum, ulnarly the lunate and capitate. Pitfall: waist fractures are occult on standard axial planes—reformat along the scaphoid long axis; retrograde blood supply makes proximal-pole fractures prone to avascular necrosis and nonunion.

Scapula.note: The Fossa glenoidea articulates with the humeral head, and the acromion and Processus coracoideus project above it. The suprascapular nerve runs through the suprascapular and spinoglenoid notches. Pitfall: an os acromiale (an unfused acromial apophysis persisting into adulthood) can look like an acromial fracture. Look for its smooth, corticated margins.

Second metacarpal bone.note: The notched base locks against the trapezoid, trapezium, capitate and third metacarpal; extensor carpi radialis longus inserts dorsally and flexor carpi radialis palmar on the base. Pitfall: a carpal boss (os styloideum) at the dorsal 2nd/3rd CMC junction mimics a fracture fragment or osteophyte; it is corticated and well-defined.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
Proper palmar digital branches of median nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of hand

Second metatarsal bone.note: The basis is recessed between the three cuneiforms (the keystone) and is tied to the medial cuneiform by the Lisfranc ligament. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx II. Pitfall: a fleck avulsion, or a medial MT II base out of line with the intermediate cuneiform, means a Lisfranc injury. A flattened caput suggests Freiberg infraction.
passing: Medial dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of second finger of foot

Second rib.note: True rib that articulates with T1 and T2. Its cartilage meets the sternum at the angulus sterni, and the tuberositas musculi serrati anterioris lies on its outer surface. Pitfall: calcified costal cartilage near the sternum can mimic a fracture or a lung nodule. A first or second rib fracture means high-energy trauma, so check the subclavian and axillary vessels.

Sesamoid bones of foot.note: The tibial (medial) and fibular (lateral) sesamoids lie in the flexor hallucis brevis tendons under caput ossis metatarsi I. The flexor hallucis longus tendon runs between them. Pitfall: a bipartite sesamoid (usually tibial, smooth corticated halves, often bilateral) mimics fracture. Fracture edges are sharp and non-corticated.
passing: Common plantar digital branches of medial plantar nerve
neighbours: Medial head of flexor hallucis brevis
Lateral head of flexor hallucis brevis

Seventh rib.note: Last true rib. It articulates with T6 and T7, and its cartilage reaches the sternum at the xiphisternal level. The diaphragmatic dome and lower lobe lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: merged cartilages of ribs 7 and 8 at the costal margin can mimic a fracture or a mass. Follow each cartilage separately.

Sinus of frontal bone.note: Sinus ossis frontalis lies between the anterior table under the glabella and a posterior table facing the anterior cranial fossa and Gyrus rectus. The Septum sinuum frontalium is often off the midline. Pitfall: unilateral aplasia or hypoplasia is a normal variant and must not be reported as opacification or postoperative change.
landmarks: lm:Septum of frontal sinuses|Sinus of frontal bone

Sinus of sphenoid bone.note: Sinus ossis sphenoidei lies under the sella and Adenohypophysis, with the Arteria carotis interna along each lateral wall and the nasopharynx below. Pitfall: the Septum sinuum sphenoideorum often inserts on the bony carotid canal, which may be dehiscent. Report this before transsphenoidal surgery.
landmarks: lm:Septum of sphenoidal sinuses|Sinus of sphenoid bone

Sixth rib.note: True rib. Its caput costae articulates with T5 and T6, its tuberculum costae with the T6 transverse process, and the angulus costae lies lateral to the erector spinae. The neurovascular bundle runs in the sulcus costae. Pitfall: subtle buckle fractures at the angulus costae are missed on axial slices. Use curved reformats.
neighbours: Sternocostal head of pectoralis major muscle

Sphenoid bone.note: The body contains the sphenoid sinus and the sella. The greater wings form the floor of the middle cranial fossa and the lateral orbital wall, and the pterygoid processes project downward. Pitfall: on coronal images, the foramen rotundum (V2) lies superolateral to the pterygoid canal. Do not swap them, and do not mix up foramen ovale with the smaller posterolateral foramen spinosum.

Stapes.note: Basis stapedis fills the fenestra vestibuli on the vestibulum. The crura run laterally to the processus lenticularis incudis, and the tympanic facial canal lies just above. Pitfall: the crura are sub-millimetre and often not visible, so do not call them absent. Fenestral otosclerosis shows as a hypodense focus just anterior to the oval window.
landmarks: lm:Articular facet of head of stapes|Stapes

Talus.note: The trochlea fits in the ankle mortise between the tibia and both malleoli. The talus meets the calcaneus below at the subtalar facets and the navicular in front. The flexor hallucis longus runs between the lateral and medial tubercles. Pitfall: an os trigonum behind the lateral tubercle mimics a Shepherd fracture, and lateral process fractures are easily missed.
landmarks: lm:Groove for tendon of flexor hallucis longus of talus|Talus

Temporal bone.note: It has squamous, tympanic, mastoid and petrous parts. The petrous apex points toward the clivus, and the mandibular fossa holds the TMJ. Pitfall: normal fissures and sutures (petrotympanic, tympanomastoid, petrosquamous) and the vestibular and cochlear aqueducts can look like fractures. Trace them on both sides.
landmarks: lm:Anterior surface of petrous part|Temporal bone

Tenth rib.note: Lowest false rib. Its head usually has a single facet for T10 only, and its cartilage forms the lower costal margin. The diaphragm and costodiaphragmatic recess lie deep to it. Pitfall: a free-ending tenth costal cartilage (costa fluctuans decima) is a normal variant. Do not report it as a dislocation, and check the liver and spleen when this rib is fractured.

Thalamus.note: The thalamus is the paired grey-matter mass that forms the lateral wall of the Ventriculus tertius. Laterally it is separated from the Nucleus lentiformis by the posterior limb of the internal capsule. Anterolaterally it is bordered by the Nucleus caudatus and the floor of the Ventriculus lateralis, and inferiorly it continues into the Mesencephalon. Its supply comes mainly from perforators of the Arteria cerebri posterior. Pitfall: on CT, physiological calcification of the Glandula pinealis, habenula and Plexus chorioideus next to the posterior thalamus can be mistaken for haemorrhage or a calcified thalamic lesion. Small lacunes can also be confused with dilated perivascular spaces.

Third metacarpal bone.note: The base articulates with Os capitatum and has small facets for metacarpals II and IV. The dorsoradial styloid process takes the Extensor carpi radialis brevis insertion, and the head forms the third MCP joint. Pitfall: a carpal boss or os styloideum at the dorsal base can look like a fracture fragment or an osteophyte.
passing: Dorsal digital branches of radial nerve
neighbours: Proximal phalanx of third finger of hand

Third metatarsal bone.note: The basis articulates with the lateral cuneiform and with MT II and MT IV. The caput articulates with proximal phalanx III. Pitfall: an early march (stress) fracture of the corpus is often occult. Count the rays from MT I to avoid labelling the wrong metatarsal.
passing: Intermediate dorsal cutaneous nerve of foot
Dorsal digital branches of superficial fibular nerve

Third rib.note: True rib that articulates with T2 and T3. Pectoralis minor attaches anteriorly, and the upper lobe and pleura lie on its inner surface. Pitfall: counting ribs anteriorly or on axial slices alone often shifts the number by one. Count from the first rib on coronal or 3D reformats and cross-check with the thoracic vertebrae.

Thyroid cartilage.note: The two Laminae cartilaginis thyreoideae meet anteriorly at the Prominentia laryngea and enclose the paraglottic space. The Cornua inferiora articulate with the cricoid. Pitfall: unossified segments of irregularly ossified cartilage mimic erosion or tumour invasion. A calcified triticeous cartilage beside the Cornu superius is not a fracture fragment.

lm:Inferior horn of thyroid cartilage|Thyroid cartilage

Tibia.note: The tibial plateau bears the femoral condyles. The fibula meets the tibia at both tibiofibular joints, and the talus articulates with the facies articularis inferior and malleolus medialis. Pitfall: the oblique nutrient canal in the posterior proximal shaft mimics a fracture. Posterior malleolus fractures are easily missed without sagittal reformats.

Trapezium bone.note: It has a saddle facet for metacarpal I distally, Os scaphoideum proximally, and Os trapezoideum and the base of metacarpal II on the ulnar side. The palmar Tuberculum ossis trapezii borders the FCR groove. Pitfall: fractures of the trapezial ridge are often missed on radiographs, so check the axial CT. Do not confuse the trapezium (thumb ray) with the trapezoid.

Trapezoid bone.note: This wedge-shaped bone is wider dorsally. It articulates with the base of metacarpal II distally, Os scaphoideum proximally, Os trapezium radially and Os capitatum ulnarly. Pitfall: overlap on radiographs hides its rare fractures, and dorsal ridges at the CMC II–III joints (carpal boss) can look like avulsion fragments.

Triquetrum bone.note: Os lunatum lies radially, Os hamatum distally and Os pisiforme on the palmar side, with the TFCC proximal to it. The dorsal cortex is the usual site of avulsion fractures, best seen on sagittal images. Pitfall: an os triangulare or an ununited fragment of the ulnar styloid can look like an acute dorsal triquetral chip.
passing: Dorsal carpal branch of ulnar artery
neighbours: Ulnar collateral ligament of wrist joint

Twelfth rib.note: Short floating rib on T12 with no tubercle articulation. Quadratus lumborum and the diaphragm attach to it, and medially the posterior pleural recess extends below it. Pitfall: a hypoplastic twelfth rib versus a lumbar rib on L1 leads to vertebral miscounting. Count from C2 or T1 and state the numbering method.

Ulna.note: Proximally, the Incisura trochlearis holds the humeral trochlea and the Incisura radialis holds the radial head. Distally, the Caput ulnae sits in the sigmoid notch under the TFCC. Pitfall: the normal transverse bare area across the trochlear notch can look like a fracture line.
neighbours: Articular disc of distal radio-ulnar joint
Ulnar head of extensor carpi ulnaris

Upper canine.note: The upper canine (FDI 13/23) has a long root that rises in the canine eminence next to the nasal floor and the canine fossa of the Maxilla. Pitfall: impaction, usually on the palatal side, is common. Localise the canine in 3D and check for root resorption of the adjacent lateral incisor.

Upper first molar tooth.note: Three-rooted molar (two buccal roots, one palatal) in the processus alveolaris maxillae. Its roots indent the floor of the sinus maxillaris. Pitfall: thin or dehiscent bone over the root apices is a normal finding. Focal mucosal thickening at the sinus floor above a periapical lucency points to odontogenic sinusitis, not rhinogenic disease.

Upper first premolar.note: Premolar in the processus alveolaris maxillae, distal to the canine eminence. It is usually two-rooted (buccal and palatal). Pitfall: the second, palatal root is easy to miss on axial slices. Check coronal reformats when you assess periapical lesions or a residual root.

Upper lateral incisor.note: The upper lateral incisor (FDI 12/22) lies between the medial incisor and the canine in the premaxillary alveolus, below the nasal floor. Pitfall: it is often absent or peg-shaped, which is a normal variant. The alveolar cleft in cleft patients lies between this tooth and the canine; do not miscount the teeth.

Upper medial incisor.note: The upper medial incisor (FDI 11/21) flanks the midline, with the incisive canal between the two roots on the palatal side. Pitfall: a wide incisive canal or nasopalatine duct cyst can mimic a periapical lesion, and a midline supernumerary tooth (mesiodens) can be mistaken for an impacted incisor.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery

Upper second molar tooth.note: Molar with often fused roots, sitting near the tuber maxillae and the processus pyramidalis of the os palatinum. It is often the tooth closest to the floor of the sinus maxillaris. Pitfall: fused or convergent roots can be misread as a single root or as root resorption. Assess them on oblique or coronal reformats.

Upper second premolar.note: Usually single-rooted tooth between the first premolar and the first molar in the processus alveolaris maxillae. Its apex often lies just under the sinus floor. Pitfall: the anterior recess of the sinus maxillaris projecting over the apex mimics a periapical lucency. Look for an intact lamina dura on sagittal reformats.

Vomer.note: It forms the posteroinferior bony nasal septum. It sits on the nasal crests of the maxilla and palatine bone, its alae wrap the sphenoid rostrum, and its anterosuperior edge meets the ethmoid perpendicular plate and septal cartilage. Its free posterior edge divides the choanae. Pitfall: a septal spur at the vomer–cartilage junction is not a fracture.
passing: Posterior septal branches of sphenopalatine artery
Septal branches of posterior ethmoidal artery
Anterior septal branches of anterior ethmoidal artery

Zygomatic bone.note: It articulates with the frontal, maxillary, temporal and sphenoid bones at four sutures, and a zygomaticomaxillary complex fracture disrupts all four. It forms the lateral orbital rim and floor. Pitfall: normal sutures and the zygomaticofacial foramen can look like fractures. Compare with the other side for diastasis or a step-off.
landmarks: lm:Zygomatic process of temporal bone (tip)|Temporal bone
lm:Orbital surface of frontal bone|Frontal bone
